title: Permission Models for Autonomous Systems
summary: Autonomy isn't binary. Reach and initiative are different questions, and the layer most models skip is whether an agent should act on its own or wait.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Whether an agent can reach a system and how much initiative it gets once it's there are two different questions, and most permission models only ever answer the first one.** A grant either exists or it doesn't. Nothing in that structure says whether the agent should act on its own or stop and wait for a person.


That gap is why a permission that looks perfectly reasonable on paper still produces an incident nobody meant to allow. The action was authorized. Nobody had decided whether it should run unattended.


We think the fix is to treat autonomy as its own axis, separate from what an agent is allowed to touch. A suggestion, a draft, a reversible execution, and an action nobody can walk back are four different risk profiles wearing the same authorization.


This isn't an argument for slowing every agent down with a checkpoint. It's the opposite: knowing which actions are cheap to get wrong is what lets you leave the rest running on their own.


Sort your agent's actions by what happens if they're wrong, not by which system they touch. The tier each one lands in tells you how much autonomy it's earned.


## Overview


Traditional software performs predefined actions through predictable paths. A payroll system runs the payroll job. A ticketing tool moves a ticket through fixed states. What the software can do is enumerated by its developers, and a user's permissions just gate which of those fixed paths they're allowed to trigger.


Agents don't work that way. A single agent can interpret a request, choose which tools to call, chain several steps together, and land on an action nobody wrote down in advance. Two people asking the same question can send the same agent down entirely different sequences. That's the whole point of building one, and it's also why a grant that answers "can this agent reach the system" tells you almost nothing about what happens once it does.


This post is about the layer most permission systems skip because reach and access don't require it: how much initiative an agent should be trusted with, and under what conditions that trust holds.


**The core shift:** a static grant answers whether an action is allowed. It says nothing about whether the agent should take it without asking first.


## Why Agents Are Different


We don't think you can secure an agent by enumerating its workflows, because the workflows are generated at runtime rather than written down in advance. That doesn't mean agents need unlimited freedom. It means the thing you're securing has to be the boundary of what an agent may attempt, not a fixed list of paths.


Most existing access-control thinking, roles, scopes, who can reach what, still applies and still matters. What it doesn't cover on its own is a second question that has nothing to do with reach: given that an action is fully allowed, should it happen automatically, or should a person see it first? An agent that's perfectly safe drafting a document can be dangerous the moment it's allowed to send, publish, or delete without anyone looking.


## Reach Is Not the Same as Initiative


Getting reach and access right is its own discipline, covered in depth elsewhere in this series: which tools an agent can connect to at all, which actions it can take inside each one, which specific records are in scope, and whose authority it's acting under when a person is involved. Those four questions answer "what could this agent possibly do."


A quick shape of it, since the rest of this post builds on it: a procurement agent might reach the vendor catalog and the contracts repository and nothing else. Inside those tools it can read and draft, not approve or delete. The records in scope are its own department's, not every department's. And when it's acting for a specific buyer, its effective reach narrows to whatever that buyer is separately allowed to do.


None of that tells you whether the agent should act the moment it decides to, or whether someone should look first. That's a fifth question, orthogonal to all four above, and it's the one the rest of this post is about.


## Autonomy Level


Even when an action clears every reach and access check, one thing is still undecided: should the agent perform it automatically, or pause for a person? Authorization says the action is allowed. Autonomy level says how much initiative the agent gets in exercising it, and it's the layer most systems built for human users never had to define.


Think of it as a dial rather than a switch:


- **Suggest:** the agent proposes an action but takes none. A recommendation a person enacts.
- **Draft:** the agent prepares the work product, an email, a config change, a record, but stops short of committing it.
- **Execute with approval:** the agent is ready to act, but a checkpoint gates the final step.
- **Execute autonomously:** the agent acts on its own, appropriate for actions that are low-risk and easy to undo.


The right level is rarely uniform across a single agent. An IT-operations agent might restart a stateless service on its own, drain a node only with a checkpoint, and merely suggest a firewall change. The dial is set per action. The riskier or harder to undo, the more a person stays in the loop.


## Context


The autonomy dial isn't fixed forever either. The same action can be fine in one circumstance and wrong in another, and a static grant can't tell the difference on its own.


A sales agent might apply a discount up to ten percent on its own, but anything past that needs a person. A data-pipeline agent might run transformations freely during business hours and get blocked from a full reprocessing job during month-end close. An action's size, its timing, and how many records it touches are all worth checking at the moment it's attempted, not just once when the grant was configured.


```text
action: opportunity.apply_discount
when discount_pct <= 10:  execute_autonomously
when discount_pct <= 25:  execute_with_approval
when discount_pct > 25:   deny
```


Context is what keeps the dial honest as circumstances change, instead of locking in whatever seemed safe the day someone set it.


## The Autonomy Spectrum


Put autonomy level and context together and one principle falls out: autonomy is not binary. Most enterprise agents sit somewhere in the middle, assisting, drafting, executing within bounds, and the same agent can land at different points on the spectrum for different actions it takes.


**Figure 1 — Reversibility, not the tool or the data touched, is what should decide where an action sits on the autonomy dial.**


The job of a permission model is to keep four things distinct that older, human-shaped systems lump together: a suggestion, where nothing changes; a draft, staged for review; a reversible execution; and an irreversible action, an external send, a deletion, a payment, a public release. The further along that list an action sits, the tighter the reach and access layers should be around it too. A suggestion needs almost none of that scrutiny. An irreversible action deserves all of it at once.


**Reversibility is the cheapest risk signal available.** The question worth asking isn't "is this allowed." It's "can this be undone." And an action that can't should always cost a person's attention.


## Putting It Into Practice


**Start from the action, not the agent.** Catalog what an agent can attempt, sort by reversibility, and set the autonomy dial per action rather than per agent. A recruiting agent reading a candidate pipeline and the same agent sending a rejection email are different risk decisions, even sharing a tool grant.


**Enforce at the boundary, not in the prompt.** The autonomy dial should live where the agent meets the system, the gateway, the tool adapter, not as an instruction the model is asked to follow. A prompt telling an agent not to send external email is a suggestion to the model. A denied action is a guarantee.


**Make the decision auditable.** When an action runs, the record should capture which autonomy level governed it and whether a checkpoint was required. That's what lets you tune the dial with evidence instead of guesswork, loosening where checkpoints are never rejected, tightening where they routinely are.


We think most teams get the first two habits right and skip the third, because auditability doesn't stop an incident. It just gives you evidence for the next decision instead of a guess.


## Conclusion


Autonomous systems need permissions with enough resolution to distinguish a suggestion from an irreversible action, and a model that sets initiative independently from reach for each thing an agent might do.


The goal isn't powerless agents. It's matching initiative to what an action actually costs if it goes wrong. An agent that drafts freely, executes the reversible on its own, and pauses for the irreversible is both genuinely useful and genuinely safe, and getting there has less to do with locking down more of the system and more to do with knowing which actions actually deserve the lock.


**Most permission models answer whether an action is allowed. The ones that hold up under real autonomy also answer whether it should happen without anyone watching.**
